### CVE-2026-126617 — Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection') in hMailServer
- Assigner: GitLab | Published: 2026-11-11 | Updated: 2026-11-17 | Max CVSS: 8.8
- CWE: CWE-89 CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
- CVSS 3.1 (cna): 8.8 HIGH `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`
- SSVC (CISA-ADP): Exploitation=none, Automatable=no, Technical Impact=total
- CVSS 3.1 (nvd:cve@gitlab.com:Secondary): 8.8 HIGH `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`

SQL injection in the database layer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.2.18, when the server uses MySQL/MariaDB or PostgreSQL, allows a remote attacker to alter SQL statements the server runs. On those two engines parameters are not bound: SQLStatement::GenerateFromCommand wrote each value into the statement's text as a quoted literal with a separate string replacement over the whole text per parameter, so a value holding the name of a parameter substituted after it had that name replaced, inside the value, by the later value with its own quotes, which ended the literal early and placed the later value in the statement as SQL. The row the server writes for each recipient of a queued message carries the recipient's address twice, so in the default configuration an authenticated user who may send mail reaches it by sending to an address of their choosing. A remote unauthenticated sender reaches the same statement through a message the server sends to the envelope sender, such as a delivery failure notice or an automatic reply, and, when greylisting or message indexing is enabled (both are off by default), through the greylisting record's envelope addresses or through the message metadata the server stores for IMAP SORT, which carries four header fields of a received message. An altered statement runs with the privileges of the server's database account; on PostgreSQL, whose client call runs every statement in the text it is given, further statements can follow it, while on MySQL/MariaDB, where one statement is run per call, the change is confined to the statement it is in. SQL Server and SQL Server Compact, where parameters are bound, are not affected.

**solutions:** Upgrade to hMailServer 6.2.19 or later, which substitutes parameters in a single pass that never re-examines a value already written into the statement, and gives each parameter a name no other parameter's name and ordinal can form. There is no complete workaround for earlier versions on MySQL/MariaDB or PostgreSQL, since the recipient row is written for every queued message; keeping message indexing (MessageIndexing) and greylisting off, as they are by default, removes those two paths only. SQL Server and SQL Server Compact installations need no action for this issue.

Affected:
- Progressive Robot Ltd / hMailServer: affected 6.0.0-B1 <=6.2.18 (semver)

### CVE-2026-126621 — Improper Certificate Validation in hMailServer

- CVSS 3.1 (cna): 7.5 HIGH `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`

Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0-B1 through 6.3.7 on Windows hands OpenSSL the names of its own TLS files - the listeners' certificates, chains, private keys and Diffie-Hellman parameters, a port's client-certificate CA file (from 6.2.19), the object store's CA file (from 6.3.4) and the ACME client's keys and certificates - as Latin-1 bytes, which on code page 1252 are the code page's own for U+00A0 to U+00FF, and OpenSSL's file opening on Windows reads a name as UTF-8 first and opens the file at that reading when it is there, or creates it there when its folder is. Until then, name every TLS file, the ACME directory and the program and data folders by paths in ASCII alone, which read as the same name in the code page and in UTF-8 and which every affected version hands over unchanged; where a name outside ASCII must stay, keep each of its characters at or below U+00FF and one the system code page writes as its Latin-1 byte (on code page 1252, U+00A0 to U+00FF; none under a UTF-8 code page) - change any other name to ASCII - and make sure no one else can create the file or folder that the name's UTF-8 reading names.

Against the released reader, one such object of 16 MB took about 5 seconds to read in the Linux build, and one of under 6 MB about 23 seconds in the Windows build, where objects of the same sizes with other names took under a tenth of a second. A remote unauthenticated attacker reaches the reader by mailing such an object as a TLS-RPT report, up to 16 MB once decompressed, to a hosted domain's report mailbox, where an administrator has set one; it is read on a mail delivery thread (ten by default), and those threads deliver all mail, local and outbound, so a stream of such reports stops all delivery for as long as it continues. It is also reached without an account through the reply to a password-protected message, with the message's link alone, where the REST API is on (it is off by default) and a public base URL for such links is set; and by any account through the webmail's routes granted 16 MB, and by an application's API key through the send API. Each such request holds one of the REST API's four worker threads, in the process that also serves SMTP, IMAP and POP3.

**solutions:** Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, whose JSON reader keeps an object's member names in an ordered set, whose cost does not depend on which names are chosen, and holds a REST request body and a mailed TLS-RPT report to 10,000 members in an object; the reply to a password-protected message is held to 2 MB. Until then, clear each domain's report mailbox, or move it off the domains the server hosts, so that no report is read by the server; and switch OpenPGP in the webmail off (portal_enabled under /api/v1/settings/openpgp), and off for any domain or account that holds openpgp_portal_enabled on, which refuses the reply to a password-protected message before its body is parsed; clearing the public base URL is not enough, since links already made stay usable. For the routes that take an account or an API key, only limiting who can reach the REST API avoids it (RestApiPort 0, the default, turns it off), or a reverse proxy in front of it that holds request bodies well below 16 MB. Restarting the service ends a busy thread.

Affected:
- Progressive Robot Ltd / hMailServer: affected 6.3.6 <=6.3.7 (semver)

Credits: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)

### CVE-2026-126624 — Unverified Ownership in hMailServer
- Assigner: GitLab | Published: 2026-11-11 | Updated: 2026-11-17 | Max CVSS: 7.3
- CWE: CWE-283 CWE-283: Unverified Ownership
- CVSS 3.1 (cna): 7.3 HIGH `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`
- SSVC (CISA-ADP): Exploitation=none, Automatable=no, Technical Impact=total
- CVSS 3.1 (nvd:cve@gitlab.com:Secondary): 7.3 HIGH `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`

Unverified ownership in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.7 allows a local authenticated user to run code as the mail server's service account or as an administrator when setup installs into, or upgrades, a program folder that accounts other than the administrators could write before, such as one made beforehand at the root of a drive. 6.3.7 fixed CVE-2026-107571 by giving the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel permissions that only administrators may change, but setup refused nothing that was already in them, or in the folders that hold the event script, the add-ons and the database scripts: a program, a library, a script or a settings file that another account owns, or whose own permissions let another account change it, is kept with that owner and those permissions, which the hardening of the folders does not take away. Setup then runs programs from Bin with the administrator's elevated rights, and the service, which runs as LocalSystem or as its virtual account, runs them and the event script, so that a library such an account placed in Bin is loaded in place of the system's; the account can still change the file after the installation. The default installation under Program Files is not affected.

**solutions:** Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.8, whose setup looks, before it stops the service and again once the folders are hardened, at everything in Bin and ControlPanel, on the program folder's own level, and in Addons, Events, DBScripts, WebAdmin, Languages and MySQL, and refuses with exit code 7 to install where a program, a library, a script, a settings file or a folder there is owned by anybody but SYSTEM, the Administrators or TrustedInstaller, has an owner that cannot be read, or has an entry of its own that lets another account change it, naming each with the icacls that deals with it and a restart of Windows before setup runs again. Until then, install hMailServer under Program Files, or into a new folder inside one that only administrators may change. Before running setup into or over a program folder that other accounts could write, list the owners from an elevated Command Prompt - dir /q /a "<program folder>" and dir /q /s /a over its Bin, ControlPanel, Events, WebAdmin, DBScripts, Addons, Languages and MySQL, as the hMailServer documentation, ServiceAccount.md, "Before upgrading an installation at a drive's root", gives them for all but MySQL - and the entries of their own, with icacls "<program folder>" and icacls "<folder>" /T over the same folders, where an entry not marked (I) that gives anybody but SYSTEM, the Administrators or TrustedInstaller a right to change the item is another account's (the service's own Modify on hMailServerApiKeys.ini in Bin apart); where anybody but those owns anything there, or has such an entry, do not install over it: reinstall into a new folder as that page's "Reinstalling into a new folder" says.

Affected:
- Progressive Robot Ltd / hMailServer: affected 6.3.7

Credits: Found by the hMailServer project (Progressive Robot Ltd)
